No need to collect every postal address, buy 150 stamps, stuff envelopes or queue at the post office. Your invitation is shared simply, without any of the paper logistics.
Schedule, venue, timings, dress code, accommodation, wedding RSVP… your guests find every useful detail straight from their phone, all in one place.
WhatsApp, SMS or email: your online wedding invitation is shared in seconds and your guests can open it straight away.

chapters_list.title: Your wedding, all in one place
chapters_list.body: Follow your digital wedding invitation in real time. RSVPs, confirmed guests, pending replies, seating plan and wedding-day preparation: your dashboard brings together everything essential about your wedding, without juggling files and tools.

chapters_list.title: Guest management made simple
chapters_list.body: Your guest list, organised by household. Families, couples or individual guests: each household is grouped with its contact details and RSVP status. Replies sent from your digital wedding invitation are gathered automatically in your space.

chapters_list.title: Build your seating plan in a few moves
chapters_list.body: Seat your guests easily, table by table. Guests who have confirmed appear in your space. Simply drag them onto the table of your choice to build and adjust your seating plan.

chapters_list.title: On the day, everyone finds their table
chapters_list.body: A QR code lets your guests find their seat in seconds. They enter their name and see their table straight away. Depending on the options you choose, they can also reach the schedule, the menu or the wedding photo-sharing space.

chapters_list.title: Track your invitation replies in real time
chapters_list.body: A clear view of your RSVPs and of attendance at each moment of the wedding. Ceremony, dinner, party or brunch: see at a glance who will be there and get the numbers you need to organise your reception and brief your suppliers.

items.question: Can I edit my invitation after sending it?
items.answer: Yes. It is one of the great advantages of a digital wedding invitation. If a detail changes after you have sent it — timings, venue, shuttles, accommodation, the schedule or any practical information — the content can be updated without having to send your guests a new invitation. The link stays the same.

items.question: Is there a subscription?
items.answer: No. Your invitation is a one-time payment, made when you create it. You choose your package at that point, and there is no monthly subscription to keep using your digital invitation throughout the period it is live.

items.question: How does the online wedding RSVP work?
items.answer: Your guests can confirm their attendance straight from your digital wedding invitation. Depending on your project, the RSVP form can also gather further details such as menu choices, food allergies, whether they will join the brunch, transport needs or other bespoke questions. Everything is then gathered in one place, so that organising your wedding and chasing replies is easier.

items.question: How long does my invitation stay accessible?
items.answer: Your invitation stays accessible for the period set out in your package. We confirm that period when you place your order. During that time, your guests can return to the schedule, the venues, the practical details and their invitation from the same link.

items.question: Can I use a custom domain name for my invitation?
items.answer: Yes, depending on the package you choose. Your invitation can be given its own web address, for an experience even more closely in keeping with the identity of your wedding. This option can be included in the most personalised services in particular.

items.question: Do you offer a paper version?
items.answer: The Studio specialises in digital wedding stationery. The aim is to create an interactive invitation, designed for mobile, that brings together everything your guests need to know. That experience can nonetheless be complemented by a printed piece carrying, for example, a QR code that leads to your digital invitation.

items.question: What is a digital wedding invitation?
items.answer: A digital wedding invitation is an invitation you open online from a link, designed first and foremost to be viewed on a phone. Unlike a simple image sent by message, it can bring together several interactive modules: countdown, schedule, venue, dress code, accommodation, RSVP, playlist, car sharing, FAQ or photo gallery. It becomes both an invitation and a genuine organising tool.

items.question: How do I send a digital wedding invitation to my guests?
items.answer: Your digital wedding invitation can be sent simply by WhatsApp, SMS or email. It can also be opened through a QR code printed on a Save the Date, a card or signage. Your guests have nothing to download: they open the invitation straight from their phone.

items.question: Can I add a QR code to my wedding invitation?
items.answer: Yes. A QR code can be added to a printed piece, leading straight to your digital wedding invitation. It can be used on a Save the Date, an invitation card, a welcome sign or another piece of stationery. The QR code gives your guests instant access to your interactive invitation and your online RSVP.

items.question: What information can an interactive wedding invitation include?
items.answer: An interactive wedding invitation can bring together everything your guests need before the wedding day: date, countdown, schedule, venues, directions, dress code, accommodation, dietary requirements, RSVP, playlist, car sharing, FAQ, gifts or practical details. Each element can be presented in its own module, so that the experience stays clear and a pleasure to browse.

items.question: What is the difference between a digital invitation and a wedding website?
items.answer: A wedding website exists mainly to gather information in one place. A digital invitation is conceived first as an invitation: it creates a first impression, introduces the world of the wedding and carries the guest through to their RSVP. It is generally shorter, more immersive, more editorial and designed more as a mobile experience.

items.question: Does the invitation work on every phone?
items.answer: Invitations by The Studio are designed mobile first, so they are easy to read on a phone. The text, animations, buttons and modules are all designed to give a smooth experience, with no app to install.

faire-part-mariage-digital.metaTitle: Digital wedding invitations: how they work
faire-part-mariage-digital.metaDescription: How a digital wedding invitation works: shared by link, RSVP built in, a QR code for print, and content you can correct after sending.
faire-part-mariage-digital.lede: A digital wedding invitation is not a picture of an invitation sent by message. It is a web page in your names that opens from a link, reads on a phone, and holds the invitation and the planning in one place. Here is what that changes.

sections.title: What it actually is
sections.body: A page at its own web address. Your guests get that link by message, or scan it from a printed QR code. Nothing to download, no account, no app — the phone's browser is enough. That is the real difference from a PDF or an image: a page can hold a form, a map, a countdown, and it can be changed after you have sent it.

sections.title: Three collections, not a template
sections.body: Ciao Amore borrows from the Amalfi Coast — bright lemon, deep olive, sun-washed pastels. Blanc Couture is the collection of almost nothing: white, fine gold, a great deal of air. Belle Rive is the most generous, mother-of-pearl and olive leaves, built for weddings that run over several days. Each one opens as an interactive demo, with real content, before you choose.

sections.title: What the RSVP form can ask
sections.body: You decide the questions: a plus-one, children, dietary needs, attendance at the next-day brunch or the welcome dinner, a lift, a free-text message. An adults-only wedding shows no children field at all — not a disabled one, none. Answers land in your account, filtered by status and exportable for your caterer.

sections.title: The modules your wedding needs
sections.body: Countdown, hour-by-hour schedule, venue and directions, dress code, accommodation, transport, menu, a playlist your guests add to, guest book, gift list, photo gallery, FAQ. Each becomes a section of the invitation, and you take only the ones your day calls for.

sections.title: Editable from your account
sections.body: After sending, you keep control of the content: times, accommodation, dress code, the FAQ. The invitation's link does not change, so there is nothing to resend to anyone. It is why your guests go back to it in the week of the wedding instead of writing to you.

sections.title: A single payment
sections.body: You pick your package when you create the invitation, and it is a one-time payment — no monthly subscription to keep using it while it is live. Three levels, from a personalised collection to a design drawn entirely around your wedding.

faire-part-mariage-digital.faqTitle: What if we want something printed too?
faire-part-mariage-digital.faqBody: The two complement each other better than they compete. A printed card carrying a QR code keeps the gesture — the envelope you open — and points to the full invitation for everything practical. Your account generates your invitation's QR code, ready to hand to your printer.

que-mettre-faire-part-mariage.metaTitle: What to include in a wedding invitation
que-mettre-faire-part-mariage.metaDescription: What to write on a wedding invitation: the details that must be there, what can wait, and the wording that works.
que-mettre-faire-part-mariage.h1: What to include in a wedding invitation
que-mettre-faire-part-mariage.lede: An invitation has to answer four things before anything else: who is marrying, when, where, and how to reply. Everything after that is comfort — useful, but secondary. Here is how to rank it, and where the invitation should stop.

sections.title: The four details that are not optional
sections.body: Both your names, the full date including the year, the town and the venue, and how to confirm. That is the floor: a guest with those four can hold the date and start planning. Include the year even for a near date — an invitation received in November for a wedding in June is genuinely ambiguous without it.

sections.title: Separating the moments and the guests
sections.body: This is the most common and most awkward mistake. If your day runs a ceremony, a dinner, a party and a brunch, and not every guest is invited to all of it, the invitation has to say so plainly. A guest arriving for dinner when they were expected at the party is a situation nobody wants to handle on the day. Phrase it positively: "We would love to see you for the evening, from 9pm" reads better than an implied exclusion.

sections.title: The practical details that stop the questions
sections.body: Dress code, parking, nearby accommodation, arriving by train or car, whether children are welcome, the gift question. None is essential to the announcement; all of them save you messages. On paper they end up as loose insert cards that get lost. In a digital invitation each becomes a section you consult when you need it — a guest looking for the venue address the night before knows where to look.

sections.title: The RSVP: what to ask on the first pass
sections.body: Attendance, obviously. But also whatever you will need for the caterer and the logistics and would hate to chase separately: the number of guests, allergies or dietary needs, the brunch, a lift. One question asked at the right moment is worth three follow-ups.

sections.title: Tone: short, personal, and yours
sections.body: The formal constructions inherited from official correspondence say nothing to anyone now. One sentence that sounds like you beats a paragraph of convention. "We said yes. All that is missing is you" works because it is direct and it sets the tone of the party. Write the sentence you would say to a friend on the phone, then cut it in half.

sections.title: What not to put on it
sections.body: Internal running order (when the photographer arrives), anything that will change (the weather, a shuttle number), and anything that belongs to a family negotiation. An invitation announces and invites; it does not arbitrate. Moving details belong in a digital invitation precisely because they can be corrected there without resending anything.

que-mettre-faire-part-mariage.faqTitle: Should the gift registry go on the invitation?
que-mettre-faire-part-mariage.faqBody: Convention is still to leave it off the invitation itself. In a digital invitation it can live in its own section, which a guest opens if they want to: available without being pushed, which settles a subject that is always slightly delicate.

quand-envoyer-faire-part-mariage.metaTitle: When to send wedding invitations: the full timeline
quand-envoyer-faire-part-mariage.metaDescription: Save the date, invitation, RSVP deadline, follow-ups: the real timeline for sending wedding invitations, month by month.
quand-envoyer-faire-part-mariage.h1: When to send your wedding invitations
quand-envoyer-faire-part-mariage.lede: The short answer: invitations go out four to six months ahead, save-the-dates nine to twelve months ahead if your guests have to travel. But the real question is not the send date — it is the date you need the answers by.

sections.title: Count back from the deadline, not the wedding
sections.body: Your caterer wants a final number by a certain date — often three to four weeks out. Your follow-ups take two to three weeks. Your guests need three to four weeks to answer. Add it up: your invitation has to go out at least two and a half months before the wedding, and that is a floor, not a target. Set the RSVP deadline first, then place the send date.

sections.title: Nine to twelve months: the save-the-date
sections.body: It only earns its place in three cases: a wedding abroad, a full weekend that costs guests annual leave, or a busy season where they are choosing between events. It holds the bare minimum — your names, the date, the region, and the fact that a full invitation follows. A save-the-date that says too much makes the invitation redundant.

sections.title: Four to six months: the full invitation
sections.body: This is the window where a guest can still book a reasonable train and arrange time off. Earlier and they note the date and forget to reply. Later and you collect refusals caused by conflicts they could have avoided. For a peak-season wedding in a tourist region, aim for six: your guests' accommodation needs booking too.

sections.title: Two to three months: tracking the replies
sections.body: The thankless phase. Out of a hundred guests, expect a third to answer in the first week, a third after one nudge, and the last third to need individual effort. This is where structured tracking earns its keep: The Studio invitations show every guest as confirmed, declined or awaiting, filterable, with an export — you chase the right people without rereading three group chats.

sections.title: One month: targeted follow-ups
sections.body: Chasing everyone is the surest way to annoy the people who already replied. Contact only the guests still outstanding, and by name — a personal message gets an answer, a group message dissolves. It is also the moment to collect what is missing: a guest may have confirmed without mentioning a dietary need.

sections.title: The week of the wedding: the invitation still works
sections.body: A paper invitation finished its job months ago. A digital one has not: this is when guests go back to check the time, the address, the dress code, the shuttle. You can still correct a last-minute detail — the link does not change, and nobody receives contradictory information.

quand-envoyer-faire-part-mariage.faqTitle: Can you send an invitation too early?
quand-envoyer-faire-part-mariage.faqBody: Yes. Beyond eight months, with no particular reason, guests note the date and postpone replying indefinitely — you lose the benefit of the notice and chase more. If you want to communicate early, a save-the-date does that job better than a full invitation sent prematurely.

textes-faire-part-mariage.metaDescription: Thirty wedding invitation wording examples, from the most restrained to the most direct, with what makes each one work.
textes-faire-part-mariage.lede: Good invitation wording is short and sounds like you. Here are thirty lines grouped by register — to take, to cut, to mix. They work because none of them is trying to sound ceremonial.

sections.title: Direct and contemporary
sections.body: "We said yes. All that is missing is you." · "It's official: we're getting married." · "Our next chapter starts here, and you're in it." · "Come and celebrate our best decision." · "After all this time: yes." · "We have a date. We have a place. We want you." — This register works because it says one thing. Resist adding a second explanatory sentence.

sections.title: Restrained and elegant
sections.body: "We would be glad to have you with us." · "A promise, a party, a memory to make together." · "Join us as we begin our life together." · "We're getting married, and we would love you there." · "On the day we say yes, we would like to see you." · "Your presence matters to us that day." — The safest register for an invitation spanning several generations.

sections.title: Warm and personal
sections.body: "You have mattered in our story; we want you in this chapter." · "Come laugh, dance and celebrate with us." · "We want to mark this with the people who count. You're one of them." · "There will be music, people, and a great deal of feeling. Come." · "That day, we would like to be surrounded. By you." — Best when the guest list is short and every name counts.

sections.title: Minimal
sections.body: "Us. You. A date. A party." · "One answer: yes." · "To the two of us, and with you." · "Two names, one date, one place." · "Yes." · "The date is set." — These need a layout that carries them: plenty of white space, one strong typeface. On a busy composition they read as an oversight.

sections.title: Written for a digital invitation
sections.body: "Scroll down, it's all here." · "Your invitation starts here." · "The schedule, the venue, and your reply: below." · "Everything you need to know, on one page." · "Welcome to our day." · "Give us thirty seconds and we'll explain everything." — These use what a web page allows: announcing there is more, and guiding towards the reply.

sections.title: How to choose and adapt
sections.body: Write the sentence you would say to a friend, without thinking about it. Compare it to the examples above: yours is probably better, just slightly too long. Cut the opening. Then check it works out loud and leaves no doubt about who is marrying. One last test: if the line could belong to any couple, it is too generic for yours.

textes-faire-part-mariage.faqTitle: Should the parents be named in the wording?
textes-faire-part-mariage.faqBody: It is a traditional usage that remains common, and sometimes expected by families. Nothing requires it in the announcing line itself: a digital invitation can name the parents in a section of its own, which honours the convention without weighing down the opening.

gerer-rsvp-mariage.metaTitle: How to track wedding RSVPs without a spreadsheet
gerer-rsvp-mariage.metaDescription: Tracking replies, dietary needs, follow-ups and a final headcount without rebuilding a spreadsheet by hand.
gerer-rsvp-mariage.h1: Tracking wedding RSVPs without a spreadsheet
gerer-rsvp-mariage.lede: The problem with RSVPs is not receiving the answers: it is knowing, at any given moment, who has not replied and what is missing. A spreadsheet manages that — at the cost of manual entry that starts again with every message.

sections.title: Why the spreadsheet gives out
sections.body: It does not fail in principle, it fails on updates. Replies arrive by message, text, email, phone and in person over dinner. Each needs entering. Three weeks in, two people are holding two versions of the file, someone has answered on behalf of their partner, and nobody knows whether "Martin" is confirmed or merely enthusiastic. The mistake is not using a spreadsheet — it is hand-copying a stream that arrives continuously.

sections.title: One point of entry
sections.body: The useful shift is having the guest reply where they read the invitation, in a form. The answer is recorded as they typed it: their name, their attendance, their party, their dietary needs. No transcription, so no transcription error. Replies to The Studio invitations arrive straight in your account.

sections.title: The three statuses that matter
sections.body: Confirmed, declined, awaiting. The third is the only one that needs action, and it is the one a spreadsheet hides: an empty row looks as much like a missed entry as an absent reply. Your RSVP view filters by status, which turns "who is left to chase?" into a glance rather than a reread.

sections.title: Asking for what you need on the first pass
sections.body: Every detail you do not collect at RSVP time will have to be chased individually later. Allergies and dietary needs, the exact number of adults and children, attendance at the brunch or welcome dinner, a lift: asked in the form, they are answered alongside attendance. Chased in April across forty people, they take an evening.

sections.title: Your guests type, you type nothing
sections.body: The reply is stored as the guest wrote it — their name, their party, their dietary needs. You transcribe nothing, so you introduce no transcription error, which is the main flaw of manual tracking and it disappears. Your account shows the current list at all times, without anyone maintaining a file.

sections.title: Reusing the answers downstream
sections.body: The RSVP is not an end: its data feeds the final headcount for the caterer, the dietary list for the kitchen, the shuttle sizing, the seating plan. Exporting your guest list saves rebuilding by hand what you have already collected.

gerer-rsvp-mariage.faqTitle: What about guests who never reply?
gerer-rsvp-mariage.faqBody: Make a phone call, and treat silence as a decline at the deadline you announced. That is what the deadline is for: without one, you wait indefinitely. Build the margin into the conversation with your caterer rather than into your nerves.

sections.heading: 9. Applicable law and disputes
paragraphs: These Terms are governed by French law. In the event of a dispute, an amicable solution will be sought before any legal action. Failing an amicable agreement, the French courts shall have sole jurisdiction.
Contact: [contact email to complete]

sections.heading: 1. Data controller
paragraphs: The controller responsible for processing personal data collected on this site is [Company name to complete], with registered office at [address to complete], reachable at [contact email to complete] (hereinafter "The Studio Digital Papeterie").

sections.heading: 2. Data collected
paragraphs: As part of the use of the Service, we collect in particular: the Customer's identification and contact details (first name, last name, email address); information relating to the wedding and guests entered in the configurator and dashboard (guest names, households, tables, RSVP responses, dietary requirements, messages); payment data, processed exclusively by our provider Stripe; technical browsing data (cookies, IP address, connection logs). When you use the contact form, we collect the information you enter: first name, last name, e-mail address and, if you provide them, your wedding date and location, the approximate number of guests, the collection you are interested in, how far along your project is and the content of your message. The date of your consent is also recorded.

sections.heading: 3. Purposes of processing
paragraphs: This data is collected in order to: provide and customize the Service (creation of the invitation and invitation website); manage the contractual relationship and payment of the order; enable the collection and management of guest responses (RSVP) on behalf of the Customer; provide customer support; comply with our legal and accounting obligations.

sections.heading: 4. Legal basis
paragraphs: Processing is based, depending on the case, on the performance of the contract concluded with the Customer, on consent (in particular for non-essential cookies), or on compliance with a legal obligation.

sections.heading: 5. Hosting and subcontractors
paragraphs: Data is hosted by Supabase (database and authentication) and payments are processed by Stripe. These providers may process data outside the European Union, subject to appropriate safeguards (standard contractual clauses or equivalent).
Messages sent through the contact form are delivered to us by e-mail via our sending provider Resend.
Site host: [hosting provider to complete].

sections.heading: 6. Retention period
paragraphs: Data is retained for the period necessary to provide the Service, plus the legal retention periods applicable in commercial and accounting matters, after which it is deleted or anonymized.

sections.heading: 7. Data sharing
paragraphs: Guest data entered by the Customer (particularly RSVP responses) is visible to the Customer in their dashboard. It is neither sold nor transferred to third parties for commercial purposes. It may be shared with our technical subcontractors (hosting, payment) strictly to the extent necessary for the performance of the Service.

sections.heading: 8. Cookies
paragraphs: The site uses cookies that are strictly necessary for it to work, which do not require your consent. It may also set, only after you agree, audience-measurement and advertising cookies intended to understand site traffic and measure campaigns. No non-essential cookie is set before you have made your choice. You can accept or decline these cookies in the consent window shown on your first visit, and change your choice at any time via the "Manage cookies" link in the footer.

sections.heading: 9. Data subject rights
paragraphs: In accordance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), everyone has the right to access, rectify, erase, restrict, object to, and port their data, as well as the right to lodge a complaint with the relevant supervisory authority (in France, the CNIL, www.cnil.fr).
These rights may be exercised by writing to [contact email to complete].

sections.heading: 10. Security
paragraphs: The Studio Digital Papeterie implements reasonable technical and organizational measures to ensure the security and confidentiality of personal data, in particular through encryption of data in transit and restricted access policies (RLS) on the database.
